title: Can I turn a folder of product footage into consistent silent clips?
summary: Prepare a consistent set of silent product clips by defining shared transformations, separating exceptions, and keeping one output per source.
body_markdown:
## What you’ll take away


- Use batching for a shared operation, not for different editorial decisions disguised as one task.
- Keep a clean source-to-output relationship.
- Define trim boundaries around the action instead of assuming every clip starts the same way.


## Define what consistent means for this delivery


A consistent set might share orientation, output dimensions, absence of live sound, and a naming convention. It does not necessarily need identical duration or speed. A rotating object and a hand demonstrating a feature may require different amounts of time to be understood.


For an illustrative website delivery, the client wants one silent file per product action. Some clips contain crew conversation, some begin before the action, and a few are rotated incorrectly. Those are useful batch-preparation tasks, provided you state exactly which operation applies to which group.


## Separate a uniform batch from exceptions


Group files that genuinely share the same treatment. If only some need rotation, keep them in a separate set. If one clip's live audio explains the product, decide whether the silent version needs a visual label or a different source before stripping it.


Do not use one aggressive trim rule for a folder with varied action timing. A fixed opening offset works only when the source setup supports it. Otherwise define the action boundary for each clip or make a manual selection. The batch should repeat a resolved instruction, not guess a different story for every file.


## Start the transformation in Wideframe


In a new chat, identify the source set and the separate output folder. The[batch-transform recipe](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/batch-transform/) describes applying an agreed set of transformations with one output per input. Copy the public recipe to add the task, then provide the exact operations and naming you need.


Keep original footage available. The website-ready clips are derivatives, not replacements for the full source. A later request may need the original audio, a longer action, or a different crop. Clear output naming makes that relationship easy to follow.


## Trim for the visible action


Let the viewer see what changes. A button press needs its result; a product opening needs enough of the opening to explain the mechanism. Avoid beginning with a hand already covering the key detail or ending before the action resolves.


For a loop, consider whether the final state can return naturally to the opening. Not every action makes a seamless loop. A deliberate pause or a different selected segment may work better than forcing a cut that makes the product jump. Treat loop design as an editorial choice beyond simply removing audio.


## Decide whether speed changes help or mislead


A modest speed adjustment can make a repetitive motion easier to fit, but it also changes how the action appears. Do not speed a real process in a way that implies a product completes it that quickly. Use appropriate context when timing is meaningful to the claim.


Keep delicate actions readable. A short clip is not useful if the audience cannot see how the feature works. If a required runtime is too tight, narrow the action or use a clearer angle rather than accelerating everything indiscriminately.


## Deliver a set someone can identify


Use names that connect each output to the product and action. Keep variations distinguishable and avoid overwriting a previous delivery without a clear version change. Provide a concise note about which clips are exceptions or need another source.


Watch the outputs in the intended context when possible. Silent clips may rely on accompanying labels or page copy, and a website crop may hide a detail visible in the full frame. Check the actual files for unwanted audio and correct action boundaries before they leave the editing workflow.


## Reuse the batch rules on the next shoot


Save the stable transformation instructions after the first useful delivery. Keep the source group and any action-specific boundaries as current inputs. A later shoot may use different orientation or timing, so do not apply the previous rule without confirming that it still fits.


The repeatable value is preparing many similarly specified assets while retaining individual source identity. Use the editor for exceptions and the assistant for the operations that truly repeat.


## Try this request


TRY AN EXAMPLE REQUEST


For this selected set of product clips, remove the live audio and apply these exact transformations: \[operations\]. Create one output per source in a separate folder with the agreed names. Keep clips needing different action trims separate for review.
